title: gonna = going to · d'you = do you
es: En el habla rápida «going to» (de futuro) se convierte en «gonna», y «do you» en «d'you». No se escribe así en el examen, pero lo oirás constantemente.
spoken: I'm gonna grab a coffee before the lecture. D'you want one?
full: I'm going to grab a coffee before the lecture. Do you want one?

title: wanna = want to
es: «Want to» se funde en «wanna». Ojo: «wants to» (he wants to) no se reduce así.
spoken: Do you wanna come round on Saturday? We're gonna watch the match.
full: Do you want to come round on Saturday? We're going to watch the match.

title: gotta = got to · hafta = have to
es: «Have got to» y «have to» (obligación) suenan «gotta» y «hafta»: la v de «have» se ensordece delante de «to».
spoken: I've gotta finish this essay tonight, so I hafta say no.
full: I've got to finish this essay tonight, so I have to say no.

title: dunno = don't know · lemme = let me
es: Dos reducciones muy frecuentes en conversación informal.
spoken: I dunno where I left my keys. Lemme check my bag.
full: I don't know where I left my keys. Let me check my bag.

title: would've = would have
es: «Would have» suena «wudəv». Por eso hay nativos que escriben mal «would of»: es el mismo sonido. Tú escribe siempre «would have» o «would've».
spoken: I would've called you, but my phone died.
full: I would have called you, but my phone died.

title: should've · could've
es: Igual que «would've»: el «have» queda reducido a «əv».
spoken: You should've told me. I could've helped.
full: You should have told me. I could have helped.

title: it'd = it would / it had
es: «It'd» puede ser «it would» o «it had»: lo decide lo que viene detrás (infinitivo → would; participio → had).
spoken: It'd be easier if we took the train. It'd already left when we got there.
full: It would be easier if we took the train. It had already left when we got there.

title: Formas débiles: to = /tə/
es: Las palabras gramaticales sin acento se reducen a una vocal neutra (schwa). «To» suena casi «tə».
spoken: I'm going to the bank to pay in a cheque.
full: I'm going to the bank to pay in a cheque.

title: of = /əv/ · a lot of → «a lotta»
es: «Of» se reduce a «əv» o incluso a «ə»: «a lot of» suena «a lotta», «sort of» suena «sorta».
spoken: A lot of people were sort of confused by the instructions.
full: A lot of people were sort of confused by the instructions.

title: can /kən/ frente a can't /kɑːnt/
es: En afirmativa «can» casi desaparece (kən); «can't» se pronuncia entero y acentuado. Fíjate en la vocal y el acento, no en la t final, que a veces no se oye.
spoken: I can swim, but I can't dive.
full: I can swim, but I can't dive.

title: and = /ən/ o /n/
es: «And» entre dos palabras se reduce a «ən» o solo «n»: «fish and chips» suena «fish'n'chips».
spoken: Fish and chips, salt and vinegar, and a cup of tea, please.
full: Fish and chips, salt and vinegar, and a cup of tea, please.

title: was /wəz/ · were /wə/
es: En medio de la frase «was» y «were» se reducen. Solo suenan fuertes al final o en respuestas cortas («Yes, I was»).
spoken: They were waiting for ages, but she was late anyway.
full: They were waiting for ages, but she was late anyway.

title: have /əv/ como auxiliar
es: Como auxiliar, «have» se reduce: «Where have you been?» suena «where'v you been?».
spoken: Where have you been? We've been looking for you everywhere.
full: Where have you been? We've been looking for you everywhere.

title: Unión consonante + vocal: turn_it_off
es: Si una palabra acaba en consonante y la siguiente empieza por vocal, se pegan: «turn it off» suena «tur-ni-toff». Por eso parece una sola palabra.
spoken: Turn it off and put it away, please.
full: Turn it off and put it away, please.

title: Elisión: nex' day, las' bus
es: La t y la d entre dos consonantes suelen desaparecer: «next day» suena «nex' day», «last bus» suena «las' bus».
spoken: We left the next day and nearly missed the last bus.
full: We left the next day and nearly missed the last bus.

title: did you → «didja» · what do you → «whaddya»
es: La d + y se funden en un sonido «ya». «Did you» suena «didja» y «what do you» suena «whaddya».
spoken: Didja see that? Whaddya think?
full: Did you see that? What do you think?

title: don't you → «doncha»
es: La t + y se funden en «ch»: «don't you» suena «doncha», «got you» suena «gotcha».
spoken: Why doncha come with us? Gotcha, see you there.
full: Why don't you come with us? Got you, see you there.

title: kinda = kind of · sorta = sort of
es: «Kind of» y «sort of» (un poco, más o menos) se reducen a «kinda» y «sorta».
spoken: It was kinda weird, sorta like a dream.
full: It was kind of weird, sort of like a dream.

title: Golpe glótico: bo'le, wa'er
es: En muchos acentos británicos la t entre vocales se sustituye por un corte en la garganta: «bottle» suena «bo'le», «water» suena «wa'er».
spoken: Could I have a bottle of water, please? It's a bit hot.
full: Could I have a bottle of water, please? It's a bit hot.

title: R de unión: there_are, far_away
es: En inglés británico la r final no suena… salvo si la siguiente palabra empieza por vocal: «far away» suena «fa-ra-way».
spoken: The car is far away, over there on the corner.
full: The car is far away, over there on the corner.

title: 'em = them
es: «Them» se reduce a «'em»: «tell 'em», «let 'em know».
spoken: Tell 'em I'll be late, and let 'em start without me.
full: Tell them I'll be late, and let them start without me.

title: innit = isn't it · y'know = you know
es: «Innit» es muy británico e informal (sobre todo en Londres). «Y'know» es una muletilla que oirás en cualquier acento.
spoken: It's a bit expensive, innit? But, y'know, it's worth it.
full: It's a bit expensive, isn't it? But, you know, it's worth it.
